title: Should the Venue Use Facial Recognition to Speed Up Entry?
script: Dara: [thoughtful] Wulan, did you see the venue is trialing facial recognition for entry next month? No more queuing for twenty minutes with everyone's tickets on their phones.
Wulan: I saw it, and honestly, my first thought wasn't convenience, it was wondering where exactly my face ends up once it's been scanned and stored.
Dara: [carefully] They claim the data gets deleted within twenty-four hours. That seems worth it, especially compared to the chaos of last year's entrance.
Wulan: Claims are easy to make, though. What recourse would we have if that promise turned out to be loosely interpreted?
Dara: [reflective] That's fair, I suppose. I hadn't really questioned whether the policy was enforceable or just something printed on a website nobody reads.
Wulan: Exactly my concern. Once biometric data has been collected, it can't simply be reissued like a stolen password. There's no starting over with a new face.
Dara: [honestly] I see your point, although there's a difference between reasonable caution and assuming the worst of every organization adopting new technology.
Wulan: I'm not assuming malice, just asking whether convenience justifies handing over something that permanent for something that trivial, saving fifteen minutes at a gate.
Dara: [gently] Would you feel differently if attendance were entirely optional, and people could still queue the traditional way if they preferred?
Wulan: Genuinely, yes. An opt-in system changes the calculation completely, because then it's a choice rather than something quietly imposed on everyone who wants to get inside.
Dara: [calmly] That distinction hadn't occurred to me before. I'd been picturing this as purely a technical upgrade, not something with consent built into it.
Wulan: It's rarely just technical, is it? Every convenience seems to come with a quiet question attached: convenient for whom, and at what eventual cost?
Dara: [encouraging] Now I feel slightly guilty for being excited about skipping a queue. Though I still think the queue itself was borderline inhumane last summer.
Wulan: It absolutely was. I'm not opposed to solving that problem, I just want the solution to ask permission before it recognizes my face.
Dara: [seriously] Fair enough. I'll email the organizers about making it opt-in and see if enough of us can push them to reconsider.
